Reviewed Actor and SessionPrincipal types, ROLE_RANK, findPasswordHash, and the sessions schema. Also noted a double-consume issue in the rate limit logic.

The rememberMe flag is parsed but ignored; the cookie expiry always uses the 30-day session token. The login flow also consumes rate limits twice: once in loginAction and again in auth-service.login.

createSessionToken generates a 32-byte base64url token, hashes it with SHA-256, and stores the hash in the session repository. It returns only the raw token to the caller.

resolveSession hashes the token again, joins the users table, checks expiry, and returns a SessionPrincipal containing userId, email, activeOrgId, and expiresAt. The raw token and password are never returned.

The browser cookie is set as httpOnly with sameSite lax, secure in production, path /, and expiry matching principal.expiresAt. The action returns the principal JSON to the client.
I have a complete picture and am ready to write the explanation.

content.text:
Typing an email and password on the sign-in form ends with a role-filtered workspace sidebar. The password never leaves the server check, the browser only receives an opaque session cookie, and every later request rebuilds a one-organization `Actor` whose role is what the sidebar and `can()` authorize against.

## The form

`LoginForm` in `src/app/(auth)/login/login-form.tsx` is a client component. On submit it reads `email`, `password`, and `rememberMe` from the form data and runs `loginSchema` from `src/schemas/auth.ts` (`email` plus a non-empty `password`). Field errors stay in the browser. A valid payload is passed to the server action `loginAction`. The page at `src/app/(auth)/login/page.tsx` has already decided the landing path: the `next` query parameter if it is a same-site path, otherwise `/orgs`. An already-live session on that page skips the form and `redirect`s there.

## Checking the credentials

`loginAction` in `src/actions/auth/login.ts` does not use `withAction`, because there is no `Actor` yet. It parses the body again with `loginSchema`. It then calls `consumeRateLimit` against the anonymous org id and the `auth:login` bucket (`src/lib/rate-limit.ts`). A denied verdict throws `RateLimitedError`.

It calls `login` in `src/server/services/auth-service.ts`, which charges that same anonymous bucket a second time, then:

1. `findUserByEmail` in `src/server/repositories/user-repository.ts`. A missing user throws `"Those credentials did not match"`.
2. `findPasswordHash` for that user id. The stored value is a scrypt string from registration (`scrypt:<saltHex>:<keyHex>`), not the password.
3. `verifyPassword` in `src/lib/hash.ts` derives a key with `scrypt` over the NFKC-normalized password and the stored salt, then compares with `timingSafeEqual`. A missing hash or a mismatch throws the same message, so the two failures are indistinguishable.

`rememberMe` is accepted by the schema and ignored after that. Session lifetime is always 30 days.

## What is created, stored, and handed back

`login` calls `createSessionToken` in `src/server/services/session-service.ts`:

- `randomToken(32)` in `src/lib/hash.ts` mints a base64url token from 32 random bytes. That raw string is the only secret that will leave the server.
- `hashToken` SHA-256s it. `createSession` in `src/server/repositories/session-repository.ts` inserts a `sessions` row: a new id, `userId`, `tokenHash`, `expiresAt` (now plus 30 days), and `activeOrgId: null`. The password is not written again. A dump of `sessions` cannot be replayed as a login.
- The function returns `{ user, token }` to `loginAction`. The raw token is not part of the action result.

`loginAction` immediately calls `resolveSession(token)`, which hashes the token again and loads `findSessionByTokenHash`. That join with `users` returns a `SessionPrincipal` (`src/types/member.ts`): `userId`, `email`, `activeOrgId`, `expiresAt`. An expired row is `null` and becomes `UnauthorizedActionError`. There is still no role on this object.

`setSessionCookie` in `src/lib/session.ts` is the only writer of the cookie jar. It sets `taskflow_session` (`SESSION_COOKIE_NAME` in `src/schemas/session.ts`) to the raw token, `httpOnly`, `sameSite: "lax"`, `secure` in production, `path: "/"`, and `expires` equal to `principal.expiresAt`. The action result sent to the browser is `{ ok: true, data: principal }` — identity and expiry, not the token and not a password. `LoginForm` then `router.push`es to `next`.

## How a later request knows who they are

`src/proxy.ts` (Next.js 16's middleware) runs first on non-static paths. Public prefixes such as `/login` pass through. Anything else with no `taskflow_session` value redirects to `/login?next=<path>`. A present cookie only sets `x-taskflow-authenticated: 1`. The proxy cannot reach the database, so a cookie is not proof the session is live.

The dashboard layout at `src/app/(dashboard)/layout.tsx` is the signed-in check for that tree. It calls `getSessionPrincipal` in `src/lib/session.ts`:

1. `cookies()` reads `taskflow_session`. No value means `null`.
2. `resolveSession` hashes the token and looks up the row. Unknown or expired rows are `null`.
3. A second clock check drops a principal whose `expiresAt` is already past.

`null` redirects to `/login`. The default destination `/orgs` (`src/app/(dashboard)/orgs/page.tsx`) loads that same principal, calls `listOrganizationsForUser(principal.userId)`, and if there is exactly one organization redirects to `/${slug}`. Zero organizations stay on the chooser. More than one render links. This page still has only a `SessionPrincipal`. The `GET` handler at `src/app/api/auth/session/route.ts` returns the same principal fields or a 401, and never the token.

## From a bare identity to something the workspace can authorize

The tenant layout `src/app/(dashboard)/[orgSlug]/layout.tsx` turns the principal into an `Actor`:

1. `getSessionPrincipal` again. Missing principal throws `UnauthorizedActionError`.
2. `resolveOrgBySlug`. Unknown slug is `notFound()`.
3. `resolveActorForOrg(principal, orgSlug)` in `session-service.ts` loads the org, then `findMember(org.id, principal.userId)`. No row, or a status other than `"active"`, returns `null`, which this layout also treats as `notFound()`.
4. It builds `Actor`: `{ userId, orgId, role }` from the membership row (`Role` is `"owner" | "admin" | "member" | "viewer"`). `assertOrgScope(actor, org.id)` checks that the actor's org is the one just loaded. `touchLastSeen` records the visit.
5. The layout calls `assertOrgScope` once more, then `snapshotFlags(buildFlagContext(actor, org))`, and passes `org`, `actor`, and `flags` into `OrgProvider` and `DashboardShell`.

Later mutations do the same seam through `withAction` in `src/actions/_lib/with-action.ts`: `getActor(orgSlug)` or `requireActorFor(orgId)` in `src/lib/actor.ts` loads the principal, calls `resolveActorForOrg`, and throws `UnauthorizedError` or `NoMembershipError` when the session or the membership is missing. Services then call `can()` or `assertCan()` with that `Actor`. They never see the cookie.

## Why the sidebar matches the role

`DashboardShell` (`src/app/(dashboard)/[orgSlug]/_components/dashboard-shell.tsx`) renders `AppSidebar` with the actor. `AppSidebar` (`src/components/domain/nav/app-sidebar.tsx`) does not branch on `actor.role`. It calls `visibleNav(SIDEBAR_NAV, actor, flags)` and the same for `SETTINGS_NAV`, both from `src/config/nav.ts`.

Each nav item names a `PermissionAction` (and sometimes a feature flag). `visibleNav` drops an item when its flag is off, or when `can(actor, action, navResource(...))` is false. `can` in `src/lib/permissions.ts` delegates to `explain`: the actor's `orgId` must match the resource, then `ROLE_RANK[actor.role]` must be at least `ROLE_RANK` of the minimum role in `ROLE_MATRIX` (viewer 1 through owner 4). Examples: `issue:read` and `project:read` start at viewer, so those links stay; `activity:read` starts at member, so a viewer does not see Activity; billing and org deletion stay on owner. The same `can()` call in the shell hides "New project" unless `project:create` (member and above) is allowed. The sidebar the person sees is that filtered tree for the membership role in the organization they just entered.

Later mutations do the same seam through `withAction` in `src/actions/_lib/with-action.ts`: `getActor(orgSlug)` or `requireActorFor(orgId)` in `src/lib/actor.ts` loads the principal, calls `resolveActorForOrg`, and throws `UnauthorizedError` or `NoMembershipError` when the session or the membership is missing. Services then call `can()` or `assertCan()` with that `Actor`. They never see the cookie.

## Why the sidebar matches the role

`DashboardShell` (`src/app/(dashboard)/[orgSlug]/_components/dashboard-shell.tsx`) renders `AppSidebar` with the actor. `AppSidebar` (`src/components/domain/nav/app-sidebar.tsx`) does not branch on `actor.role`. It calls `visibleNav(SIDEBAR_NAV, actor, flags)` and the same for `SETTINGS_NAV`, both from `src/config/nav.ts`.

Each nav item names a `PermissionAction` (and sometimes a feature flag). `visibleNav` drops an item when its flag is off, or when `can(actor, action, navResource(...))` is false. `can` in `src/lib/permissions.ts` delegates to `explain`: the actor's `orgId` must match the resource, then `ROLE_RANK[actor.role]` must be at least `ROLE_RANK` of the minimum role in `ROLE_MATRIX` (viewer 1 through owner 4). Examples: `issue:read` and `project:read` start at viewer, so those links stay; `activity:read` starts at member, so a viewer does not see Activity; billing and org deletion stay on owner. The same `can()` call in the shell hides "New project" unless `project:create` (member and above) is allowed. The sidebar the person sees is that filtered tree for the membership role in the organization they just entered.
